## Abstract {#summary-in-brief}

@goulet2007 found that morning types received more light around dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO), whereas evening types received more light 10–12 hours later, in a subset of four morning and five evening participants with extreme DLMO timing. We examined whether similar phase-dependent differences occur in a larger sample during everyday work and free days.

We analysed near-eye melanopic light exposure from **140 MeLiDos participants, 778 participant-days and 35,949 half-hour observations**. Cyclic generalized additive mixed models compared four MSFsc quartiles across work and free days, using local clock time and circadian phase operationalized through midsleep on free days corrected for sleep debt (MSFsc). The models accounted for site, individual daily patterns, participant-day variation and photoperiod. DLMO was represented by a published group-average DLMO reference interval relative to MSFsc.

After phase alignment, extreme morning types had higher fitted exposure **9.6–11.3 hours before MSFsc, roughly 3–5 hours before the DLMO reference**, while extreme evening types had higher exposure **0.9–4.4 hours after MSFsc**. The clock-time and circadian-phase models performed similarly well in sample (ordinary R² **0.795 and 0.794**, respectively), including participant and day effects. Chronotype direction and chronotype strength together received small Shapley allocations of **0.007 and 0.012 R²** above the common daily curve. Their 95% bootstrap intervals excluded zero. Individual patterns received the largest allocation.

Similar curve shapes under MEQ and MSFsc classification in **68 participants and 379 participant-days** support robustness to the chronotype measure and its cutoffs. This sensitivity pools definite and moderate morning types and definite and moderate evening types, excluding the 72 intermediate chronotypes.

An exploratory, post hoc analysis tested whether daylight timing contributes to the phase-dependent differences, making them larger on longer days. Comparing daylengths one hour below and above each site's average, the evening-to-morning ratio of exposure changed by **−16.6% before the DLMO reference** (95% CI **−66.6% to +108.5%**) and **+159.1% after MSFsc** (95% CI **+5.9% to +534.2%**). Conceptual phase-response-curve weighting gave higher advance-weighted exposure indices in extreme evening than extreme morning types, but the group differences were not statistically significant. These indices summarize exposure timing and do not predict phase shifts.

## Background and aims

MeLiDos is a multicentre study of personal light exposure during everyday life. Participants wore light loggers near the eyes and on the chest and recorded sleep, device removal, and daily activities. A common protocol was used at nine sites in seven countries, with measurements collected between August 2023 and October 2025. Participants were recruited through the participating research groups rather than through population sampling [@zauner2026exposome].

This analysis uses prepared measurements and diary data from the [MeLiDos analysis repository](https://github.com/tscnlab/ZaunerEtAl_bioRxiv_2026) [@melidosanalysis2026]. The accompanying preprint is *The health-relevant architecture of the everyday light exposome* [@zauner2026exposome]. The imported files are included in this project, with a fixed source snapshot and checksums, so the analysis can run without a second repository checkout.

The primary question is whether chronotype differences in daily exposure persist after aligning observations to circadian phase, operationalized through midsleep on free days corrected for sleep debt (**MSFsc**). We also compare work and free days to test whether daily schedules change the exposure patterns and chronotype differences. The outcome is **melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance**, abbreviated melanopic EDI: light weighted for melanopsin sensitivity and expressed as an equivalent daylight illuminance in lux. Near-eye measurements are primary. Chest measurements provide a sensitivity check, informed by the sensor-placement study by @zauner2026placement, which found close agreement for some exposure metrics and placement-dependent differences for others. During recorded sleep, the loggers were placed near the bed, so those readings describe the sleeping environment [@zauner2026exposome].

Chronotype groups are defined by MSFsc quartiles: extreme morning, moderate morning, moderate evening and extreme evening. **Chronotype direction** distinguishes morning from evening, and **chronotype strength** distinguishes extreme from moderate groups. The median of 04:16 falls within a published MCTQ intermediate range of 04:00–04:59 [@juda2013]. The Morningness–Eveningness Questionnaire, or **MEQ**, measures preferred timing of sleep and activity [@horne1976] and provides an alternative group definition in a sensitivity analysis.

We compare local clock time with time relative to each participant's MSFsc as a sleep-based measure of individual circadian phase. **Dim-light melatonin onset**, or **DLMO**, was not measured in MeLiDos. The diagonally striped bands show a published DLMO reference interval, 6.95–5.95 hours before MSFsc, derived from the early- and late-group means in 38 healthy adults (mean age 22.7 years, SD 4.2) studied by @facerchilds2019. This interval does not estimate individual DLMO [@kantermann2015].

After examining the main results, we added an **exploratory, post hoc daylength analysis**. The hypothesis is that daylight timing contributes to the phase-dependent differences between extreme morning and evening types. Morning types reach their evening circadian phase earlier in clock time, when daylight may still be available; evening types encounter sunrise earlier relative to their own phase. If daylight contributes to these differences, the morning–evening contrast before the DLMO reference and after MSFsc should be larger on longer days and smaller on shorter days. We examine this pattern by adding daylength moderation to the phase model and by plotting civil dawn and dusk relative to MSFsc.

A second exploratory analysis asks whether the timing of light exposure is consistent with an **advancing pattern in extreme evening types and a delaying pattern in extreme morning types**. We weight the estimated exposure curves of these two groups by a published light phase-response curve (PRC) [@sthilaire2012] and integrate over 24 hours, using the DLMO reference interval to align the time coordinates. The resulting signed indices summarize exposure across phases associated with advances and delays. Comparing the published raw PRC with its drift-corrected form tests how the baseline affects this interpretation; the indices describe exposure patterns rather than measured shifts of the circadian clock.

## Data and sample

The analysis uses R 4.6.1 and the existing tested package versions, recorded in this project's `renv.lock`. The [input guide](input-data/README.md) describes the copied data and source attribution; the [snapshot manifest](input-data/manifest.csv) records their original paths, source commit and checksums. Reusable helper files handle repeated fits, contrasts, validation and attribution. Their inputs, choices and results appear below in analysis order, and the complete files are linked at the end. The small `table_data()`, `show_table()` and `show_figure()` helpers are reused throughout: they read exported tables, apply common gt formatting, and display figures. The [table-formatting code](R/report_tables.R) changes presentation only.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
source("R/setup.R")
options(sass.cache = file.path(tempdir(), "melidos-gt-sass"))
source("R/report_tables.R")
for (module in c("data", "models", "inference", "diagnostics",
                 "validation", "attribution", "plots", "sensitivity")) {
  source(paste0("R/", module, ".R"))
}
table_data <- function(name, directory = "results/tables") {
  read.csv(file.path(directory, paste0(name, ".csv")), check.names = FALSE)
}
show_figure <- function(name) {
  knitr::include_graphics(file.path("results/figures", paste0(name, ".png")))
}
```

### Prepared measurements and additional exclusions

The daily-pattern data, prepared in the source repository, supply 30-minute arithmetic-mean melanopic EDI. A bin needs at least 15 valid minutes. Zeros remain in the analysis; the response is log10(melanopic EDI + 0.1). Work/free-day labels come from the diary's waking date. We require MSFsc and a day-type label for both time representations. The source repository calls its daily-pattern analysis **H02**, originating from preregistered hypothesis 02 on within-participant versus between-site variation in hourly melanopic EDI [@melidos2026preregistration; @h02]. That identifier is retained in imported filenames for traceability.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sample-flow
#| tbl-cap: "Sample flow. Participants are counted uniquely at each step."
prepared <- prepare_data() # <1>
show_table(prepared$flow)
```

1. Join the prepared light measurements, participant information and waking-date diary labels. The shared registry records each exclusion and supplies sample counts throughout the report.

The sample flow in @tbl-sample-flow starts with **141 participants and 816 participant-days** with near-eye measurements. One participant has no MSFsc, removing 6 days. A further 32 days across 24 retained participants have no diary record for that waking date. The joint analysis therefore contains **140 participants, 778 participant-days and 35,949 half-hours**. The removed days still have light measurements; they cannot contribute to a model that requires a work/free label. The complete [day-inclusion registry](results/tables/day_inclusion_registry.csv) records these decisions.

Both models use exactly the same records (@tbl-time-coordinates) and preserve their sequence order. Clock time is the local bin midpoint. Phase is clock time minus MSFsc, wrapped over 24 hours. Negative values on the phase plots precede MSFsc.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-time-coordinates
#| tbl-cap: "Common analytical sample for the clock-time and circadian-phase coordinates."
near_eye <- prepared$frames$glasses
stopifnot(all(near_eye$clock == (near_eye$clock_bin + 15) / 60))
stopifnot(all.equal(near_eye$phase_display,
                   ((near_eye$clock - near_eye$msf_hours + 12) %% 24) - 12))
show_table(count_sample(near_eye))
```

The primary sample comprises 78 female and 62 male participants, with a median age of 27 years (range 18–68). The [demographic verification script](R/manuscript_review_checks.R) joins the frozen demographic input to the primary participant registry and exports the summary below; its [runtime record](results/provenance/manuscript_review_runtime.txt) documents inputs and R/package versions.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-primary-demographics
#| tbl-cap: "Sex and age of the 140 primary near-eye participants."
show_table(table_data("primary_demographics"), digits = 0)
```

### Chronotype groups

Quartiles use one MSFsc value per participant, so each person contributes equally. We use R's default quantile calculation (`type = 7`): after sorting the values, it locates the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles and interpolates linearly between adjacent values when a percentile falls between them. Values equal to a boundary stay in the earlier quartile, so ties are never split. The cutoffs are fixed across work/free days and sensor placements.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cutoffs
#| tbl-cap: "MSFsc quartile boundaries."
cutoffs <- quantile(distinct(near_eye, participant_key, msf_hours)$msf_hours,
                   c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75), type = 7)
show_table(table_data("quartile_cutoffs") |>
  select(percentile, msf_hours, clock_time),
  labels = c(msf_hours = "MSFsc (hours)", clock_time = "Clock time"))
```

The boundaries are 03:10, 04:16, and 05:15 (@tbl-cutoffs). A published Munich ChronoType Questionnaire (MCTQ) classification places MSFsc from 04:00 to 04:59 in an intermediate range [@juda2013]. This supports moderate-morning and moderate-evening labels on either side of the sample median. @tbl-groups summarizes the resulting groups.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-groups
#| tbl-cap: "Four chronotype groups. Times are MSFsc; counts refer to the complete near-eye sample."
groups <- table_data("quartile_distribution")
groups[c("minimum", "median", "maximum")] <-
  lapply(groups[c("minimum", "median", "maximum")], clock_label)
show_table(groups)
```

The recorded MEQ categories provide a useful comparison (@tbl-meq-overlap). The two measures are related but describe different aspects of chronotype. Here, 18 of 34 people in Q2 and 23 of 36 in Q3 are intermediate by MEQ. Group classifications from MSFsc, MEQ and DLMO can disagree [@reiter2021].

```{r}
#| label: tbl-meq-overlap
#| tbl-cap: "MSFsc quartiles and recorded MEQ categories. Each cell shows participants / participant-days."
meq_order <- c("Definitely morning type", "Moderately morning type",
               "Intermediate", "Moderately evening type",
               "Definitely evening type")
meq_overlap <- table_data("quartile_meq_overlap") |>
  mutate(sample = paste(participants, participant_days, sep = " / ")) |>
  select(quartile, meq_type, sample) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = meq_type, values_from = sample, values_fill = "0 / 0") |>
  select(quartile, all_of(meq_order))
show_table(meq_overlap)
```

{{< include notes/chronotype-distributions.qmd >}}

@tbl-day-support gives the work/free-day counts available within each quartile.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-day-support
#| tbl-cap: "Work/free-day support in the near-eye (glasses) sample. A participant may contribute to both day types."
show_table(table_data("group_day_counts") |>
  filter(placement == "glasses") |>
  select(-placement))
```

## Model specification

The models extend the source study's daily-pattern analysis [@zauner2026exposome; @h02] by making every daily curve cyclic: the end of one day joins smoothly to the start of the next. They use Gaussian errors on the transformed response and the R package `mgcv`'s discrete `bam()` fitting with fast restricted maximum likelihood (fREML) [@wood2017; @wood2017large]. Each model has a common daily curve, quartile and day-type deviations and their interaction, site deviations, individual random curves, participant-day random intercepts, and photoperiod effects.

All daily curves are cyclic cubic splines. The sum-to-zero `sz` basis estimates curve effects for categorical groups, including quartile, day type and site; the deviations sum to zero across the relevant factor levels. The `fs` basis supplies smooth random participant effects around those shared curves. Population/group/site bases use `k = 12`, participant bases use `k = 10`, and photoperiod uses a cubic regression spline with `k = 5`. The time-by-photoperiod interaction uses `ti()` with marginal dimensions `k = c(12, 5)`. Photoperiod is the **duration from civil dawn to civil dusk**, calculated using the **suntools** package through the `LightLogR::photoperiod()` wrapper. It is centered using the mean over distinct dates within each site.

```{r}
#| label: model-specification
formula_used <- model_formula()
formula_used
```

The `sz` terms include level effects, so no duplicate quartile, day-type or site intercepts are added. The standard `sz` penalties are estimated separately. In the installed `mgcv` version, linking the cyclic `sz` penalties with `id` produced a numerical rank failure; removing `id` retained `sz`, its sum-to-zero constraints, and cyclic cubic margins.

A separate [basis-sensitivity notebook](noncyclic-sz-sensitivity.html) compares these models with noncyclic cubic margins for every `sz` term. It retains the cyclic common curve and the original participant `fs` and time-by-photoperiod `ti()` structures, isolating the change to categorical-group curves. The primary models remain unchanged. Ordinary in-sample R² changes by less than 0.0001 on either time coordinate. The noncyclic group curves introduce small jumps at midnight or, for the phase model, at MSFsc; the overall endpoint intervals include continuity. The post-MSFsc extreme-group interval remains, from **0.92 to 4.25 hours**, with an average evening/morning factor of **13.24**. The earlier interval no longer excludes a factor of one under the simultaneous bands, so its inferential status is sensitive to the endpoint specification. The repeating daily pattern therefore retains cyclic group curves in the primary specification.

The quartile-by-day model estimates all eight group/day curves. Chronotype direction, chronotype strength and their interactions are contrasts of those curves. For attribution subsets, direction alone or strength alone receives its corresponding two-level smooth; when both are present, the four-level quartile smooth is used. A day-type interaction enters only with its contributing non-interaction factors, so it is interpreted together with their effects.

A preliminary fit checks the mean structure before estimating the residual correlation between adjacent observations. The first-order autoregressive correction, AR(1), follows elapsed time in UTC and resets at every participant-day, missing interval, gap and ambiguous daylight-saving link. Phase wrapping does not reorder observations.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-fitted-models
#| tbl-cap: "Fitting summary for the two near-eye models."
preprocessing <- fit_preprocess(near_eye, prepared$cutoffs)
# Reuse only fits with matching data and formula signatures.
clock_model <- fit_pair(near_eye, preprocessing, "clock", "primary")
clock_summary <- model_summary(clock_model)
rm(clock_model); invisible(gc())
phase_model <- fit_pair(near_eye, preprocessing, "phase", "primary") # <1>
phase_summary <- model_summary(phase_model)
rm(phase_model); invisible(gc())
show_table(bind_rows(clock_summary, phase_summary) |>
             select(axis, rho, edf, convergence, participants,
                    participant_days, half_hours))
```

1. Fit the same model to the same observations using circadian phase in place of clock time. Only the time coordinate changes; chronological ordering and the rules for residual correlation stay the same. Matching saved fits can be reused.

## Model checks and sensitivity

The fitted-model summary is given in @tbl-fitted-models. Diagnostics precede interpretation; @tbl-diagnostics gives the overview. The saved checks cover convergence, basis adequacy, residual distribution, spread, residual patterns, concurvity, sequence-specific autocorrelation, cyclic continuity, and participant/site influence. Gratia supplies the visual diagnostic bundle and coefficient simulation [@simpson2024].

```{r}
#| label: tbl-diagnostics
#| tbl-cap: "Diagnostic summary for the two near-eye models. Flags identify checks needing attention."
diagnostics <- table_data("diagnostic_verdicts") |> filter(model == "primary")
show_table(diagnostics |>
  select(axis, convergence_ok, basis_flag, standardized_lag1,
         spread_ratio, cyclic_ok, participants, participant_days, half_hours))
```

The large global spread ratios mainly reflect the response floor and the concentration of observations there. Zero exposure maps to **`log10(0 + 0.1) = −1`**, and **31.6% of half-hours are exactly zero**. Raw residuals therefore have a lower boundary of `−1 − fitted`, producing an asymmetric pattern at low exposure. Across fitted-value deciles, the raw residual-SD ratios are **5.64 for clock and 5.91 for phase**. Rebuilding deciles among positive observations reduces them to **1.19 and 1.17**; restricting instead to fitted exposure of at least 1 lux gives **1.40 in both models** (@tbl-floor-check). These checks associate most of the global spread pattern with the floor, rather than large variance changes throughout positive exposure. They do not directly validate coverage of the full Gaussian model's uncertainty bands, which remain approximate near the boundary.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-floor-check
#| tbl-cap: "Residual-spread checks for the unchanged near-eye models, fitted to 140 participants and 778 participant-days. Each diagnostic stratum uses its own fitted-value deciles; the retained half-hours are shown. Ratios divide the largest decile SD by the smallest; innovations incorporate the fitted AR correction. These are diagnostic restrictions, not refitted analyses."
floor_checks <- table_data("revision_floor_audit_spread_summaries", "results/provenance") |>
  filter(fit_kind == "primary", stratum %in% c("all", "positive", "fitted_at_least_1_lx")) |>
  select(axis, stratum, half_hours, raw_sd_ratio, innovation_sd_ratio) |>
  mutate(stratum = recode(stratum, all = "All observations",
    positive = "Observed EDI > 0 lux", fitted_at_least_1_lx = "Fitted EDI ≥ 1 lux"))
show_table(floor_checks, labels = c(stratum = "Diagnostic stratum",
  raw_sd_ratio = "Raw residual SD ratio", innovation_sd_ratio = "AR innovation SD ratio"))
```

The [R floor audit](results/provenance/revision_floor_audit.R), with [checks for the additional models](results/provenance/revision_floor_extensions.csv), also checks exposure thresholds and adjacent observations within the original AR sequences. The variance-weighted fits below remain sensitivity checks; the original Gaussian model is the common reference for the reported candidate intervals.

High concurvity between individual curves and population/group curves is expected because the individual curves can reproduce parts of the population pattern. Penalization separates these terms. Attribution therefore describes this fitted decomposition; it does not identify independent biological contributions.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Concurvity and cyclic joins

@tbl-concurvity describes overlap among model components, and @tbl-continuity checks that values and slopes meet at the daily boundary.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-concurvity
#| tbl-cap: "Concurvity diagnostics; values near one indicate overlapping model components."
concurvity <- bind_rows(lapply(c("clock", "phase"), function(axis) {
  table_data(paste0("primary_", axis, "_concurvity"), "results/diagnostics") |>
    mutate(axis = axis, .before = 1)
}))
show_table(concurvity |> filter(.type == "estimate"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-continuity
#| tbl-cap: "Endpoint and first-derivative checks across the 24-hour join."
show_table(bind_rows(lapply(c("clock", "phase"), function(axis) {
  table_data(paste0("primary_", axis, "_cyclic_continuity"), "results/diagnostics") |>
    mutate(axis = axis, .before = 1)
})), digits = 7)
```

:::

The sensitivity fits increase the daily basis to 18 and the participant basis to 14, move `rho` by ±0.10, remove the site with the most concentrated quartile distribution, remove the participant with the largest residual RMSE, and apply variance weights. Cutoffs stay fixed. Predictions use the original common photoperiod distribution and day-type weights, so changes compare the same estimand.

@tbl-sensitivity quantifies how the registered contrasts change under each sensitivity scenario.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sensitivity
#| tbl-cap: "Sensitivity of registered contrast estimates. Changes are in log10(melanopic EDI + 0.1)."
sensitivity <- table_data("sensitivity_summary")
show_table(sensitivity |>
  select(axis, sensitivity, maximum_contrast_change, rms_contrast_change,
         deleted, convergence, participants, participant_days, half_hours))
```

The variance-weighted fits have AR-innovation SD ratios of **5.01 for clock and 3.66 for phase** across all observations, falling to **1.57 and 1.51** among positive observations. Weighting does not remove the response boundary, and these global ratios should not be read as evidence of a general variance failure. The two-step weights are estimated from the data, with uncertainty that the usual coefficient covariance does not include; they remain a sensitivity analysis rather than a demonstrated correction to the reference model.

Site deletion does show a material sensitivity: removing Kumasi (KNUST) leaves **125 participants and 697 participant-days** and changes registered contrast estimates by up to **0.38 log10 units for clock and 0.34 for phase**. Separately, only **43 of 140 clock-model peaks and 41 of 140 phase-model peaks** meet the declared timing-localization rule (@tbl-individual-timing). For the others, the fitted curve is more informative than a precise peak time. A comparison restricted to sites with both chronotype groups would address site composition more directly, but has not been fitted here.

## Daily exposure patterns

The main curves set site, participant and participant-day effects to zero, representing the average of these effects on the fitted log scale. They average over one common distribution of within-site-centered photoperiod, giving each participant equal weight and each of that participant's observed days equal weight. Overall curves also use the same pooled participant-weighted work/free mixture in every chronotype group.

For the primary exposure curves, 10,000 joint coefficient draws form 95% simultaneous bands across all 12 quartile-by-day-context curves and the 10-minute grid within each time coordinate. Clock time and MSFsc-relative time are treated separately.

Intensity curves and their bands are back-transformed with `10^estimate - 0.1` and shown in lux. The **symlog axis is linear up to 1 lux and logarithmic above 1 lux**, following the approach to visualizing zero-containing light-exposure data described by @zauner2025zeros. These are back-transformed standardized log-scale means. Small negative bounds from the Gaussian model remain visible. The fitted response remains `log10(melanopic EDI + 0.1)`.

The panel arrangement follows the clock-versus-phase comparison in @goulet2007. That paper used MEQ groups and measured DLMO to distinguish phase extremes. Here both the groups and the phase coordinate use MSFsc. The implications of these differences are discussed in @sec-comparison-goulet.

@fig-patterns-overall, @fig-patterns-work and @fig-patterns-free show overall, work-day and free-day comparisons with a common layout and explicit participant and participant-day counts for each curve. **A identifies clock time and B identifies circadian phase, expressed as hours relative to MSFsc.** Columns distinguish moderate from extreme chronotype strength.

### The published DLMO reference interval

Facer-Childs et al. report group means for MSFsc and DLMO in Table 1 [@facerchilds2019]. Their offsets place DLMO approximately 6 to 7 hours before MSFsc (@tbl-dlmo-reference). The diagonally striped vertical band spans those two group-average offsets.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dlmo-reference
#| tbl-cap: "Group-mean times and offsets used for the DLMO reference, in decimal hours. MSFsc and DLMO are local clock times; the final column gives their difference. These are reference-study values, not MeLiDos measurements."
reference_times <- tibble(
  group = c("Early", "Late"),
  MSFsc = c(2 + 24/60, 6 + 52/60),
  DLMO = c(20 + 27/60, 23 + 55/60)
) |> mutate(hours_relative_to_MSFsc = ((DLMO - MSFsc + 12) %% 24) - 12)
show_table(reference_times)
```

MSFsc and DLMO can be strongly related across people, but the offset varies between individuals. Kantermann et al. found an MSFsc-DLMO correlation of 0.68 and a substantial DLMO range at a given MSFsc [@kantermann2015]. Reiter et al. found a weaker relationship and limited agreement between chronotype categories [@reiter2021]. The reference interval is labelled **DLMO reference**. It represents literature-based group means; the circadian-phase axis remains anchored to MSFsc.

## Difference curves and candidate intervals

The comparisons were defined before fitting: evening minus morning within each chronotype-strength group; extreme minus moderate within each chronotype direction; free minus work within each quartile; three two-way interaction contrasts; and the three-way interaction. The first two sets include overall, work and free-day comparisons, giving 20 registered contrast curves per time representation.

Each curve is evaluated every 10 minutes. Ten thousand joint coefficient draws form 95% simultaneous bands over all 20 registered contrasts and times within each time coordinate. Clock time and MSFsc-relative phase address separate, literature-based questions: differences in daily schedules and differences after phase alignment. We therefore define each coordinate as a separate inferential family, without an additional adjustment across the two models. The bands account for inspecting the full contrast family and phase or clock-time grid within that coordinate; nearby times remain correlated. Smoothing-parameter covariance corrections are included when available [@wood2016]. These intervals condition on the estimated AR parameter and quartile boundaries. @tbl-inference records the covariance treatment.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-inference
#| tbl-cap: "Inference settings and analytical samples."
inference_settings <- bind_rows(lapply(c("clock", "phase"), function(axis) {
  table_data(paste0("primary_", axis, "_inference_metadata"))
}))
show_table(inference_settings |>
  select(axis, axis_family_coverage, covariance, draws, critical, free_day_weight,
         participants, participant_days, half_hours))
```

Support is assessed in local half-hour bins. We require at least four participants in every contributing quartile/day cell; this is an analyst-chosen support rule, not a published threshold. A time point enters an interval claim only if it passes that rule. Interval tables count unique participants and days with observed bin midpoints inside that interval. Intervals crossing midnight or the phase boundary are merged.

The difference plots show **factors for melanopic EDI + 0.1**, calculated as `10^contrast`, with the same transformation applied to the uncertainty bounds. The logarithmic factor axis places **1 at no difference, 2 at twice, and 0.5 at half** the reference value. The reference is morning for evening/morning comparisons, moderate for extreme/moderate comparisons, and work days for free/work comparisons. Interaction contrasts become ratios of ratios; 1 means no interaction. This display preserves the registered contrasts, support rules and simultaneous-band inference.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-interval-tables
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Prepare the interval tables"
windows <- bind_rows(lapply(c("clock", "phase"), function(axis) {
  table_data(paste0("primary_", axis, "_significant_windows"))
}))
windows_display <- windows |>
  mutate(start_label = if_else(axis == "clock", clock_label(start), sprintf("%.2f", start)),
         end_label = if_else(axis == "clock", clock_label(end), sprintf("%.2f", end)),
         positive_sample = paste(positive_participants, positive_days, positive_half_hours, sep = " / "),
         negative_sample = paste(negative_participants, negative_days, negative_half_hours, sep = " / ")) |>
  select(axis, contrast, description, context, direction, start_label, end_label,
         wraps_boundary, duration_hours, mean_log10_difference = mean_difference,
         factor_at_mean_difference = mean_ratio,
         positive_sample, negative_sample)
show_interval_table <- function(pattern) {
  selected <- windows_display |> filter(grepl(pattern, contrast)) |> select(-contrast)
  if (!nrow(selected)) {
    return(show_table(tibble(Result = "No supported candidate intervals for these comparisons.")))
  }
  show_table(selected, labels = c(direction = "Contrast sign"))
}
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

The tables in the four comparison tabs (@tbl-windows-direction, @tbl-windows-strength, @tbl-windows-day and @tbl-windows-interactions) use the same interval definitions. Each interval factor is 10 raised to the mean log-scale difference across that interval. The complete exports also include minimum and maximum differences and factors, plus every grid point's uncertainty and support. Their filenames retain `significant_windows`; the displayed tables identify them as candidate intervals under the Gaussian reference model, with the floor-related uncertainty limitation described above.

The larger timing separation is between the extreme groups. In the phase model, the reference-model bands identify extreme evening-minus-morning differences around 1 to 4 hours after MSFsc, while no supported interval overlaps the striped DLMO reference interval itself (@tbl-windows-direction). The reference interval represents published average timing rather than each participant's DLMO.

To summarize the magnitude within the two primary phase intervals, we average their contrast design vectors before applying the full coefficient covariance. This retains covariance between phase points. The 95% intervals in @tbl-primary-interval-averages treat the selected windows as fixed and are not adjusted for interval selection or multiplicity; the simultaneous bands above determine where intervals are identified.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-primary-interval-averages
#| tbl-cap: "Extreme-evening/extreme-morning interval-average exposure ratios with 95% coefficient intervals. These summaries condition on the selected windows. The exact exposure scale is melanopic EDI + 0.1."
primary_interval_averages <- local({
  bundle <- readRDS("results/models/primary_phase.rds")
  inference <- readRDS("results/data/primary_phase_inference.rds")
  interval_average_contrasts(inference, bundle)
})
save_table(primary_interval_averages, "primary_phase_interval_averages")
show_table(primary_interval_averages |>
  mutate(interval = if_else(start < 0, "Pre-MSFsc", "Post-MSFsc")) |>
  select(interval, start, end, ratio, ratio_lower, ratio_upper), digits = 2)
```

The extreme-group pattern is similar on work and free days (@fig-direction-differences). Across the early interval, **11.25 to 9.58 hours before MSFsc**, the mean evening/morning factor is **0.13 on work days and 0.21 on free days**: exposure remains lower in extreme evening types, but the difference is attenuated on free days. Across **0.92 to 4.42 hours after MSFsc**, evening-type exposure remains higher, with factors of **15.5 and 12.0**, respectively. This is a descriptive attenuation; the simultaneous bands include the no-interaction value throughout the phase cycle for both the registered chronotype-direction-by-day-type comparison and its interaction with chronotype strength (@fig-interactions). The [work/free interval summaries](results/tables/primary_phase_work_free_interval_averages.csv) retain the estimates and exploratory interval-average uncertainty.

## Individual patterns and timing

@tbl-individual-timing summarizes peak localization, and @fig-individual-timing shows individual timing uncertainty. Individual curves add each participant's fitted random curve to the same standardized group curve. Site and participant-day effects remain excluded. They use the same back-transformation and symlog lux axis as the group patterns. Peak shifts are circular differences from the corresponding group peak, using 1,000 joint coefficient draws for uncertainty. A peak is labelled localized only when its 95% circular interval is no wider than four hours and its circular concentration is at least 0.8. These are descriptive timing summaries, not fitted horizontal-shift parameters. The display transformation preserves peak locations.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-individual-timing
#| tbl-cap: "Individual timing localization by quartile. Median shift uses localized peaks only."
timing <- bind_rows(lapply(c("clock", "phase"), function(axis) {
  table_data(paste0("primary_", axis, "_individual_timing")) |>
    mutate(axis = axis, .before = 1)
}))
timing_summary <- timing |>
  summarise(participants = n_distinct(participant_key),
            localized_days = sum(participant_days[localized]),
            participant_days = sum(participant_days), half_hours = sum(half_hours),
            localized_participants = sum(localized),
            median_localized_shift = if (any(localized)) median(shift_hours[localized]) else NA_real_,
            .by = c(axis, quartile))
show_table(timing_summary)
```

Every participant's curve and contributing-day count appears in the [clock PDF](results/figures/primary_clock_individual_curves.pdf) and [phase PDF](results/figures/primary_phase_individual_curves.pdf). Full timing estimates and intervals are in the corresponding [clock CSV](results/tables/primary_clock_individual_timing.csv) and [phase CSV](results/tables/primary_phase_individual_timing.csv).

```{r}
#| label: fig-individual-timing
#| fig-subcap: ["Clock time", "Circadian phase"]
#| layout-ncol: 1
#| fig-cap: "Individual peak shifts relative to the matching group curve, with uncertainty and localization flags."
#| fig-alt: "Participant-level circular peak differences and intervals, separated by quartile and time representation."
show_figure("primary_clock_timing")
show_figure("primary_phase_timing")
```

Each factor includes the photoperiod main smooth and its interaction with time. The other model terms cancel in the comparison. A factor above 1 indicates higher fitted melanopic EDI + 0.1 than at the median photoperiod. The median reference stays at 1; pointwise bands use the covariance of each contrast with that reference.

## Fit, prediction and attribution

### In-sample fit

@tbl-fit reports the in-sample fit statistics. Adjusted R² is `mgcv`'s adjusted fit statistic. Deviance explained and ordinary R² describe in-sample fit; for these Gaussian models, ordinary R² is 1 minus residual sum of squares divided by the total sum of squares. They include fitted participant and day terms and do not measure prediction for new people.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-fit
#| tbl-cap: "In-sample fit statistics, kept separate from predictive performance and attribution."
show_table(table_data("model_fit") |>
  select(model, axis, adjusted_R2, deviance_explained, ordinary_R2,
         participants, participant_days, half_hours))
```

### Held-out prediction

Five participant-held-out folds assess new-person prediction. Assignment is balanced within site. The final observed day is separately held out for each participant with at least three eligible days, assessing prediction for known participants. The clock and phase models use identical splits. Cutoffs, photoperiod centers, smoothing and AR correlation are estimated in training data only.

New-participant predictions exclude participant and day effects. Predictions for known participants retain the participant curve but exclude the held-out day effect. Baselines use the participant-weighted training response mean. Scores give participants equal weight; paired bootstrap intervals resample participants within site and condition on the fitted folds.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-validation-samples
#| tbl-cap: "Separate training and assessment samples for every split and time representation."
show_table(table_data("validation_samples") |>
  select(target, axis, split, training_participants, training_days,
         training_half_hours, assessment_participants, assessment_days,
         assessment_half_hours))
```

Days in @tbl-validation-samples are participant-days. The [complete split table](results/tables/validation_samples.csv) also records training cutoffs, rho, and photoperiod support. Wide tables can be scrolled horizontally.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-validation-scores
#| tbl-cap: "Held-out scores on the log10(melanopic EDI + 0.1) scale. Predictive R² compares squared error with the training-mean baseline."
validation_scores <- table_data("validation_scores")
show_table(validation_scores)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-validation-paired
#| tbl-cap: "Paired phase-minus-clock score differences with 95% participant-bootstrap intervals. Negative RMSE/MAE favors phase; positive predictive R² favors phase."
paired_scores <- table_data("validation_paired_differences")
show_table(paired_scores)
```

@tbl-validation-scores reports the held-out scores. Calibration intercept and slope describe agreement between held-out observations and predictions. An ideal intercept is zero and slope is one. The paired score intervals quantify assessment-sample uncertainty; they do not repeat the full training process in each bootstrap.

**Clock time predicts new participants slightly better.** Its RMSE is 0.887 versus 0.908 for phase, with predictive R² of 0.668 versus 0.652. The paired phase-minus-clock RMSE difference is 0.0205, with a 95% interval from 0.0108 to 0.0310 (@tbl-validation-paired). For the final day of known participants, the models perform similarly: RMSE is 0.852 for clock and 0.855 for phase; the paired difference interval includes zero.

### Shapley allocation of ordinary in-sample R²

The common time or phase curve is the mandatory baseline. Seven groups enter the allocation: chronotype direction, chronotype strength, day type, site, photoperiod, participant pattern and participant-day variation. All 128 subsets per axis are fitted, with interactions only when their contributing variables are present and with the full model's `rho` held fixed. The allocation averages each group's improvement over subset orders [@azen2003]. Negative allocations, if present, are retained.

The intervals use 2,000 hierarchical site-participant-day bootstrap samples of **fixed fitted predictions**, following the source study's attribution procedure [@h02]. They are conditional on the fitted models. This is a descriptive allocation of in-sample R², distinct from a variance component or a causal contribution.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-shapley
#| tbl-cap: "Shapley allocations above the common-curve baseline, with conditional bootstrap intervals. All rows use 140 participants, 778 participant-days and 35,949 half-hours."
shapley <- bind_rows(table_data("shapley_clock"), table_data("shapley_phase")) # <1>
show_table(shapley |>
  select(axis, component, allocation, lower, upper, baseline_R2, full_R2))
stopifnot(all(abs(shapley |>
  summarise(error = sum(allocation) - (first(full_R2) - first(baseline_R2)),
            .by = axis) |> pull(error)) < 1e-9))
```

1. Combine the saved allocations from all 128 model subsets per time representation. Each component receives its average increase in ordinary in-sample R² across the allowed subset orders; the check below confirms that the allocations sum to the full-model improvement over the common curve.

@tbl-shapley and @fig-shapley show the component allocations. Participant-specific patterns receive the largest allocation above the common curve: 0.091 for clock time and 0.110 for phase. Participant-day variation is next, at about 0.042 in both models. These values describe fitted variation in this sample.

```{r}
#| label: fig-shapley
#| fig-cap: "Conditional Shapley allocation of in-sample R². Error bars are the hierarchical bootstrap intervals."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels compare the seven R-squared allocations for clock and phase."
p <- ggplot(shapley |> mutate(component = recode(component,
    direction = "Chronotype direction", extremity = "Chronotype strength")),
  aes(allocation, reorder(component, allocation))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey65") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), orientation = "y", width = 0.2) +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2") +
  facet_wrap(~axis, labeller = as_labeller(c(
    clock = "A  Clock time", phase = "B  circadian phase"))) +
  labs(x = "Allocation of ordinary in-sample R²", y = NULL,
       subtitle = sample_label(near_eye))
save_plot(p, "shapley", 11, 5)
show_figure("shapley")
```

## Exploratory daylength analysis {#sec-daylight}

Civil daylight occurs at different circadian phases across chronotypes, especially in the extreme morning and evening groups. We explore the hypothesis that this difference in daylight timing contributes to their phase-dependent light-exposure differences, producing larger contrasts on longer days. Pointwise comparisons and the interval-average contrast indicate a larger extreme-group ratio after MSFsc on longer days. This section is an additional exploration. The primary models, contrasts and attribution results remain unchanged.

### Question, model and comparison

The question is whether the extreme evening/morning exposure ratio changes with daylength, particularly during the phase intervals identified in the primary analysis: before the DLMO reference and after MSFsc. Photoperiod here means the duration from civil dawn to civil dusk, when the sun elevation is above −6°. It describes astronomical daylight availability. The measured exposure also includes artificial light and reflects indoor attenuation and participants' choices of location and activity.

We add a cyclic quartile-specific change per hour of photoperiod to the full phase model. Photoperiod remains centered within each site's observed date distribution. The common phase curve, original quartile and day-type deviations, site curves, participant curves, day intercepts and common photoperiod terms remain in the model. The added quartile change is linear in centered photoperiod and shared across work and free days. Predictions use the same pooled work/free mix as the primary comparisons and exclude site, participant and day effects.

Site adjustment is retained because dropping it could attribute differences between sites to daylength. Centering photoperiod within site draws on variation relative to each site's reference. The limited overlap of extreme chronotypes within sites still limits what this pooled comparison can establish.

The added term retains cyclic cubic `sz` smooths and their sum-to-zero constraint. In the installed `mgcv` version, a varying numeric `by` variable otherwise removes that constraint. The short wrapper below keeps the original constructor and prediction method, retains the constraint, and supplies native `sz` bookkeeping for discrete fitting. Its fitted design is checked for zero sums across quartiles, zero contribution at centered photoperiod zero, linear scaling and cyclic continuity.

```{r}
#| label: daylight-model
source("R/daylight.R")
smooth.construct.szphoto.smooth.spec
smooth.info.szphoto.smooth.spec
daylight_formula()
# This reads verified caches when available. All new artifacts have a daylight prefix.
daylight_result <- run_daylight(prepared)
```

The main figures use centered-photoperiod targets of **−1, 0 and +1 hours**. These are shorter or longer days relative to each site's mean over observed dates. We also show the participant-weighted quartiles and 10th/90th-percentile targets as sensitivities below. An observation supports a target when its centered photoperiod is within one hour. Every phase comparison requires **at least four participants** in each extreme-quartile by work/free-day cell in the corresponding half-hour phase bin. All 144 phase points pass this rule for the main targets and both sensitivities.

@tbl-daylight-scenario-samples records local support around the three targets; @tbl-daylight-model reports the expanded model fit.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-daylight-scenario-samples
#| tbl-cap: "Observations within one hour of each centered-photoperiod target. Participants can contribute to both day types and to more than one target; these counts must not be added."
show_table(table_data("daylight_scenario_samples") |>
  select(scenario, photo_target, quartile, daytype,
         participants, participant_days, half_hours))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-daylight-model
#| tbl-cap: "Expanded phase-model fit and its analytical sample. Ordinary R² and deviance explained are in-sample measures."
show_table(table_data("daylight_model_summary") |>
  select(rho, adjusted_R2, deviance_explained, ordinary_R2,
         participants, participant_days, half_hours))
```

### Model checks

The model converges, its cyclic curves join correctly, and the basis check does not call for larger dimensions. AR-standardized lag-one residual correlation is approximately **0.080**. The diagnostic plots retain the full response range, including the zero-exposure boundary discussed above.

@tbl-daylight-diagnostics summarizes these checks. @fig-daylight-model-checks, @fig-daylight-spread and @fig-daylight-autocorrelation show the residual distribution, spread and serial dependence.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-daylight-diagnostics
#| tbl-cap: "Diagnostic checks for the expanded phase model and its analytical sample."
show_table(table_data("daylight_phase_verdict", "results/diagnostics") |>
  select(convergence_ok, basis_flag, standardized_lag1, spread_ratio,
         cyclic_ok, spread_flag, participants, participant_days, half_hours))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-daylight-model-checks
#| fig-cap: "Residual checks for the expanded phase model: distribution, fitted-value pattern and spread. The model uses 140 participants, 778 days and 35,949 half-hours."
#| fig-alt: "Residual diagnostic panels show the expanded phase model's distribution and residual patterns, including unequal residual spread across fitted values."
show_figure("daylight_phase_appraise")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-daylight-spread
#| fig-cap: "Residual standard deviation across fitted-value deciles, including observations at the transformed zero-exposure boundary."
#| fig-alt: "Residual standard deviation varies strongly across the ten fitted-value groups rather than remaining constant."
show_figure("daylight_phase_spread")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-daylight-autocorrelation
#| fig-cap: "Raw and AR-standardized residual autocorrelation within true-elapsed sequences."
#| fig-alt: "Standardized residual autocorrelation is lower than raw residual autocorrelation across within-sequence time lags."
show_figure("daylight_phase_acf")
```

### Exposure patterns and changes in the group ratio

The higher phase-aligned exposure in the extreme evening group after MSFsc becomes more pronounced on longer days. For this exploratory assessment, we use 95% pointwise intervals on the 10-minute phase grid, based on the coefficient covariance with smoothing-parameter correction. Each interval addresses one phase-specific comparison; it does not provide simultaneous coverage over the complete curve. Interval-average comparisons use the covariance of the average log contrast and treat the two intervals identified by the primary 95% simultaneous bands within the phase coordinate as fixed. These comparisons are not adjusted for multiplicity or interval selection. 

@fig-daylight-patterns shows the scenario curves, @fig-daylight-ratios compares the two extreme groups, and @fig-daylight-moderation isolates the longer-versus-shorter-day change.

```{r}
#| label: fig-daylight-patterns
#| fig-cap: "Phase curves at −1, 0 and +1 hours of site-centered photoperiod. Bands are pointwise 95% intervals. Facet counts describe observed participants and days within one hour of the target; the full model uses 140 participants and 778 days. Grey windows with dashed boundaries mark the two primary phase intervals; the diagonally striped band marks the DLMO reference."
#| fig-alt: "Three panels show extreme morning and evening phase curves on shorter, typical and longer days. The evening curve rises earlier after MSFsc in all panels. Each panel gives separate participant and day counts for both groups. Grey windows with dashed boundaries mark the two primary phase intervals; the diagonally striped band marks the DLMO reference."
show_figure("daylight_phase_patterns")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-daylight-ratios
#| fig-cap: "Extreme-evening/extreme-morning ratios of melanopic EDI plus 0.1 at the three targets. Bands are 95% pointwise intervals for each phase-specific group ratio; bold segments exclude one and meet the four-person support rule. Grey windows with dashed boundaries mark the two primary phase intervals; the diagonally striped band marks the DLMO reference."
#| fig-alt: "The evening-to-morning ratio falls below one before MSFsc and rises above one after it. The later peak is higher in the longer-day scenario, with wide uncertainty bands. Bold sections mark supported pointwise intervals excluding one. Grey windows with dashed boundaries mark the two primary phase intervals; the diagonally striped band marks the DLMO reference."
show_figure("daylight_phase_contrasts")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-daylight-moderation
#| fig-cap: "Change in the extreme-group ratio from shorter to longer days. A value of one means the group ratio is unchanged. Bands are 95% pointwise intervals; bold sections exclude one and meet the four-person support rule. Grey windows with dashed boundaries mark the two primary phase intervals; the diagonally striped band marks the DLMO reference."
#| fig-alt: "The longer-to-shorter ratio of group ratios dips before MSFsc and peaks around two hours after MSFsc. Bold sections show where supported pointwise intervals exclude one. Grey windows with dashed boundaries mark the two primary phase intervals; the diagonally striped band marks the DLMO reference."
show_figure("daylight_phase_moderation")
```

Over the primary candidate interval from **0.92 to 4.42 hours after MSFsc**, the geometric mean evening/morning ratio is **7.99** at the −1-hour target and **20.69** at the +1-hour target. Their ratio is **2.59** (95% CI **1.06–6.34**), equivalent to an increase of **159.1%** (95% CI **5.9%–534.2%**). Over the earlier interval, **11.25 to 9.58 hours before MSFsc**, the corresponding change is **−16.6%** (95% CI **−66.6% to +108.5%**). The later increase is supported by this exploratory interval-average comparison, while the earlier point estimate is in the proposed direction. The bold pointwise phase comparisons exclude no change from approximately **1.17 to 3.17 hours after MSFsc**. These intervals were selected in the primary analysis and are reused here with no selection or multiplicity adjustment.

Before the DLMO reference interval, the largest estimated decrease in the group ratio occurs around **8.33 hours before MSFsc**: the longer-day evening/morning ratio is **0.41 times** the shorter-day ratio (pointwise 95% CI **0.16–1.04**). This indication of a photoperiod effect lies closer to DLMO than the primary exposure difference at **9.6–11.3 hours before MSFsc**. Its interval still includes no change; the pointwise exclusions of one occur after MSFsc.

@tbl-daylight-primary-intervals summarizes the scenario ratios within the two primary candidate intervals.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-daylight-primary-intervals
#| tbl-cap: "Scenario ratios within the two primary candidate phase intervals. Bounds are 95% conditional Gaussian intervals for each average log contrast, with the selected interval treated as fixed and no multiplicity or selection adjustment. Counts include actual observed phase midpoints within each reported interval and within one hour of the target. Each sample entry gives participants / participant-days / valid half-hours."
daylight_interval_counts <- table_data("daylight_primary_interval_samples") |>
  filter(contrast != "Longer_minus_shorter") |>
  mutate(sample = paste(participants, participant_days, half_hours, sep = " / ")) |>
  select(interval, contrast, quartile, sample) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = quartile, values_from = sample)
show_table(table_data("daylight_primary_interval_summaries") |>
  filter(contrast != "Longer_minus_shorter") |>
  select(interval, start_phase, end_phase, contrast, ratio, ratio_lower, ratio_upper) |>
  left_join(daylight_interval_counts, by = c("interval", "contrast")))
```

The complete [scenario contrast table](results/tables/daylight_contrasts.csv), [pointwise candidate windows](results/tables/daylight_pointwise_windows.csv), [interval-specific sample records](results/tables/daylight_primary_interval_samples.csv), [time-varying support counts](results/tables/daylight_local_support.csv) and the [original simultaneous windows](results/tables/daylight_significant_windows.csv) are available as CSV files. These post hoc comparisons remain exploratory.

#### Sensitivity to the daylength targets

We repeat the figures using the participant-weighted quartiles (**−0.77, 0.00 and +1.35 hours**) and the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles (**−2.17, 0.00 and +2.36 hours**). @tbl-daylight-target-sensitivities lists all three specifications. These percentiles describe centered daylength, not new chronotype cutoffs. The four-person local-support rule retains all 144 phase points in each specification, including the four morning participants near the 10th-percentile target.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-daylight-target-sensitivities
#| tbl-cap: "Centered-photoperiod targets (hours) for the main figures and two sensitivities. Percentiles give participants equal weight, then weight their observed days equally. The same 140 participants, 778 days and 35,949 half-hours supply the fitted model for every specification."
show_table(table_data("daylight_sensitivity_targets") |>
  mutate(specification = recode(specification, fixed = "Main: −1 / 0 / +1 h",
    quartiles = "P25 / P50 / P75", p10_p90 = "P10 / P50 / P90")) |>
  select(specification, scenario, photo) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = scenario, values_from = photo), digits = 2)
```

The longer-versus-shorter ratio over the primary interval after MSFsc is **2.59 (95% CI 1.06–6.34)** for the main targets, **2.74 (1.06–7.09)** for the quartiles and **8.64 (1.14–65.66)** for P10/P90. The earlier interval remains uncertain under all three choices (@tbl-daylight-interval-sensitivities). The model's photoperiod moderation is linear, so a wider target separation rescales the log contrast and its standard error together. The same phase segments therefore exclude one; the larger P10/P90 estimate comes with a much wider interval.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-daylight-interval-sensitivities
#| tbl-cap: "Longer-versus-shorter changes in the extreme evening/morning ratio within the two primary phase intervals. All intervals are exploratory 95% Gaussian intervals on the average log contrast. Local samples are printed in the corresponding sensitivity figures and retained in the scenario exports."
show_table(table_data("daylight_sensitivity_intervals") |>
  mutate(specification = recode(specification, fixed = "Main: −1 / 0 / +1 h",
    quartiles = "P25 / P50 / P75", p10_p90 = "P10 / P50 / P90"),
    phase_interval = if_else(interval == 1L, "Before DLMO reference", "After MSFsc"),
    interval_95 = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", ratio_lower, ratio_upper)) |>
  select(specification, phase_interval, ratio, interval_95), digits = 2,
  labels = c(ratio = "Ratio of ratios", interval_95 = "95% CI"))
```

@fig-daylight-quartile-sensitivity and @fig-daylight-decile-sensitivity repeat the exposure curves, group ratios and longer-versus-shorter comparisons. Bold segments identify supported pointwise intervals excluding one, using the same rule as the main figures.
