### Solar timing relative to MSFsc

We separately project each retained participant-day's civil dawn and dusk onto its participant's MSFsc coordinate. Here the shorter/longer split is **absolute civil daylength**, divided at the full sample's participant-weighted median of **13.25 hours**. This differs from the site-centered targets used in the exposure model. Within each group and absolute-daylength category, participants receive equal weight and their days receive equal weight.

@fig-daylight-civil-availability shows civil daylight availability across circadian phase; @tbl-daylight-civil-reference summarizes availability within the two primary candidate intervals.

```{r}
#| label: fig-daylight-civil-availability
#| fig-cap: "Astronomical civil daylight availability in the two extreme groups, using 70 participants and 390 participant-days. The grey vertical bands with dashed boundaries mark the primary candidate intervals before the DLMO reference and after MSFsc; the striped band marks the DLMO reference itself. Counts describe all retained days with solar metadata."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels compare civil daylight availability on shorter and longer absolute days. Grey bands with dashed boundaries mark the two primary candidate intervals, and the striped band marks the DLMO reference. Morning types have more daylight availability in the earlier interval; evening types have more in the interval after MSFsc. The availability gaps are smaller on longer days."
show_figure("daylight_civil_availability")
```

In the **primary interval before the DLMO reference**, civil daylight availability averages **100.0% for morning types on both shorter and longer days**, compared with **18.3% and 81.9% for evening types**. In the **primary interval after MSFsc**, the corresponding values are **19.7% and 69.0% for morning types**, and **81.4% and 100.0% for evening types**. Thus daylight availability separates the groups in both intervals, with smaller availability gaps on longer absolute days. These absolute-daylength summaries describe a different comparison from the within-site-centered photoperiod targets used in the exposure model.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-daylight-civil-reference
#| tbl-cap: "Mean civil daylight availability (%) within the two primary candidate intervals, evaluated on the 10-minute phase grid. All retained days with solar metadata contribute, with equal participant and within-participant day weights. Counts refer to those solar-metadata days, not only days with observed light-bin midpoints inside each interval."
show_table(table_data("daylight_civil_primary_intervals") |>
  arrange(interval, factor(daylength, levels = c("Shorter", "Longer")), quartile) |>
  select(interval_label, daylength, quartile, mean_percent,
         participants, participant_days), digits = 1,
  labels = c(interval_label = "Primary interval", mean_percent = "Daylight availability (%)"))
```

### Prediction and scope

The expanded model is evaluated in the same five participant-held-out folds as the primary phase model. Quartile cutoffs, site photoperiod centers, smoothing and AR correlation are estimated from training data. Neither participant nor day effects enter predictions for the held-out participants. Model comparisons use paired predictions on identical observations and 2,000 participant bootstrap samples stratified by site.

@tbl-daylight-validation-samples records the matched validation splits. The resulting scores and paired differences appear in @tbl-daylight-validation-scores and @tbl-daylight-validation-differences.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-daylight-validation-samples
#| tbl-cap: "Separate training and assessment samples for each participant-held-out fold. Each row uses the same split for both models; training participants and days are disjoint from assessment participants and days."
show_table(table_data("daylight_validation_samples") |>
  filter(model == "Photoperiod moderation") |>
  select(split, training_participants, training_days, training_half_hours,
         assessment_participants, assessment_days, assessment_half_hours))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-daylight-validation-scores
#| tbl-cap: "Participant-weighted out-of-sample prediction on identical held-out observations. Error measures use log10(melanopic EDI + 0.1). R² is relative to the training-mean baseline. Counts are assessment counts pooled uniquely across the five folds."
show_table(table_data("daylight_validation_scores"))
```

The expanded model's predictive R² is **0.649**, compared with **0.652** for the primary phase model. Its RMSE is **0.0044 higher**, with a paired 95% interval from **−0.0008 to 0.0100**. Adding photoperiod moderation does not improve new-participant prediction in these data.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-daylight-validation-differences
#| tbl-cap: "Paired expanded-minus-primary score differences, with 95% intervals from 2,000 site-stratified participant bootstrap samples. Positive RMSE/MAE differences favor the primary model; positive R² differences favor the expanded model."
show_table(table_data("daylight_validation_paired_differences"), digits = 4)
```

Finally, the extreme chronotypes have little overlap within individual sites: **no site has at least five participants in both Q1 and Q4**. Site curves adjust for shared site patterns, but cannot replace that missing overlap. The daylength result is a pooled exploratory association with site adjustment. It cannot establish daylight as the singular driver of the chronotype difference. A stronger test needs both extreme groups observed at the same sites across a wider seasonal range, together with information separating outdoor daylight from artificial or indoor light.

@tbl-daylight-site-composition shows the limited within-site overlap of the extreme groups.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-daylight-site-composition
#| tbl-cap: "Site composition of the two extreme quartiles. Zero rows show an absent group; only Q1 and Q4 are included."
show_table(table_data("daylight_site_composition"))
```

The [basis checks](results/provenance/daylight_basis_acceptance.csv), [independent design audit](results/provenance/daylight_independent_audit.txt), [acceptance checks](results/provenance/daylight_acceptance_checks.csv) and [primary-cache checksums](results/provenance/daylight_primary_cache_preservation.csv) document the constrained smooth, unchanged primary results and separate daylight outputs. The complete additional analysis is in [R/daylight.R](R/daylight.R).

## Sensitivity to questionnaire-based chronotype {#sec-meq}

The Morningness–Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ) measures reported preference for earlier or later activity and sleep. It offers a second way to define the comparison groups [@horne1976]. This sensitivity analysis changes **group membership**. The phase coordinate still uses MSFsc, so it does not provide a separate measurement of circadian phase.

All 140 participants in the complete near-eye sample have MEQ scores. The recorded categories agree with the conventional score ranges: 70–86 definitely morning, 59–69 moderately morning, 42–58 intermediate, 31–41 moderately evening, and 16–30 definitely evening. @tbl-meq-categories includes the full sample before restricting the sensitivity analysis.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-meq-categories
#| tbl-cap: "MEQ categories in the complete near-eye sample. Counts are unique within each row."
show_table(table_data("meq_category_sample"))
```

There are only **three definitely evening participants**, contributing 17 participant-days. A separate extreme-evening curve would be poorly supported. We therefore pool definite and moderate types within each direction and exclude the 72 intermediate participants. The fitted sensitivity sample contains **68 participants, 379 participant-days, and 17,558 valid half-hours**: 44 morning and 24 evening participants.

### Matched models and comparison sample

The pooled MEQ models use the same response, bin rules, work/free labels, cyclic spline structure, photoperiod adjustment, and true-elapsed AR(1) sequence boundaries as the primary analysis. The quartile term is replaced by a two-level MEQ chronotype-direction factor. The cyclic `sz` group and day-type deviations, their interaction, and the participant `fs` curves remain in the model. Population bases use `k = 12`, participant bases use `k = 10`, and the photoperiod basis uses `k = 5`. No extreme-versus-moderate effect is fitted in this reduced sample.

To separate the change in questionnaire from the change in sample, we also fit MSFsc models to **exactly the same observations**, dividing these participants at the original full-sample MSFsc median. These labels mean earlier and later MSFsc. Of the 68 participants, 60 retain the same direction and eight switch direction. The [classification overlap table](results/tables/meq_classification_overlap.csv) gives the participant, participant-day, and half-hour counts for each pairing.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-meq-fit-checks
#| tbl-cap: "Convergence and common sample for the paired chronotype classifications."
source("R/meq.R")
meq_raw <- meq_prepare(prepared)
meq_preprocessing <- fit_preprocess(meq_raw, prepared$cutoffs)
model_formula(k = 12L, kp = 10L)

# Each call checks the data and formula signature before reusing its fit.
meq_fit_checks <- list()
for (classification in c("MEQ", "MSFsc")) {
  for (axis in c("clock", "phase")) {
    fitted_meq <- meq_fit(meq_raw, meq_preprocessing, axis,
                          classification, k = 12L, kp = 10L)
    meq_fit_checks[[paste(classification, axis)]] <-
      model_summary(fitted_meq) |>
      mutate(classification = classification)
    rm(fitted_meq)
  }
}
show_table(bind_rows(meq_fit_checks) |>
  select(classification, axis, convergence, participants,
         participant_days, half_hours))
```

@tbl-meq-fit-checks records convergence and sample counts. In the printed formula, `quartile` is the binary morning/evening grouping for this sensitivity. The preprocessing centers photoperiod within site on the restricted sample and retains the original MSFsc cutoffs. Rendering executes these steps and checks the four cached fits. The diagnostics, standardized predictions, and contrasts below read the exports produced by `run_meq(prepared)`; rendering does not repeat the 10,000 coefficient draws. The full analytical entry point also writes the acceptance checks.

Population predictions use the restricted sample's common photoperiod distribution, with equal participant weights and equal weights for each person's observed days. Overall curves use the same work/free proportions in both groups. Site, participant, and participant-day effects are omitted from the displayed predictions.

### Model checks

All four fits converged. The basis checks did not flag an undersized basis, and the fitted curves join continuously at the daily boundary. The AR correction reduces lag-one residual correlation from about 0.62 to about 0.085. The largest raw residual standard deviation across fitted-value deciles is **7.5–8.0 times** the smallest when zeros are included, but **1.22–1.28 times** among positive observations. Restricting instead to fitted exposure of at least 1 lux gives ratios of **1.43–1.45**, consistent with a pattern concentrated near the zero boundary. High overlap among the hierarchical population, site, and participant curves also limits interpretation of isolated model terms; the full concurvity results are exported.

The response has the same zero-exposure boundary as the primary analysis, so the global spread ratio should be read in that context. These fits assess the **direction and shape** of the sensitivity results. Their candidate intervals retain the Gaussian uncertainty approximation near the boundary.

@tbl-meq-diagnostics summarizes the checks, with residual plots in @fig-meq-appraise.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-meq-diagnostics
#| tbl-cap: "MEQ sensitivity diagnostics. Each model uses the same 68 participants, 379 participant-days, and 17,558 valid half-hours. Spread ratio is the largest divided by the smallest residual standard deviation across fitted-value deciles."
show_table(table_data("meq_diagnostic_verdicts") |>
  select(classification, axis, convergence_ok, basis_flag,
         standardized_lag1, spread_ratio, cyclic_ok,
         participants, participant_days, half_hours))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-meq-appraise
#| fig-cap: "Diagnostic views for the MEQ clock-time and circadian-phase models. Each fit uses 68 participants, 379 participant-days, and 17,558 valid half-hours."
#| fig-subcap: ["Clock time", "circadian phase"]
#| layout-ncol: 1
show_figure("meq_defined_clock_appraise")
show_figure("meq_defined_phase_appraise")
```

The in-sample fits are very similar under both classifications and both time coordinates (@tbl-meq-fit). These values include participant and day effects. They do not establish which questionnaire or time coordinate predicts new observations better. Predictive validation and Shapley attribution remain focused on the primary near-eye sample.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-meq-fit
#| tbl-cap: "In-sample fit for the MEQ sensitivity and the paired MSFsc comparison. Adjusted R² is the `mgcv` estimate; ordinary R² compares residual variation with the observed response variation."
show_table(table_data("meq_model_fit") |>
  select(classification, axis, rho, adjusted_R2, ordinary_R2,
         deviance_explained, participants, participant_days, half_hours), digits = 4)
```

### Daily patterns and differences

The MEQ curves retain the main later-timing pattern: evening participants have higher exposure around late clock evening and during the rising portion of the curve after MSFsc. The same-subset MSFsc contrast has a similar shape (@fig-meq-factors). This agreement shows that these patterns are not confined to the full sample's quartile classification. It does not establish agreement between the two instruments in the full cohort, because intermediate MEQ participants are excluded here.

@fig-meq-patterns shows the fitted daily curves under MEQ classification.

```{r}
#| label: fig-meq-patterns
#| fig-alt: "Morning and evening near-eye exposure curves under MEQ classification, shown by clock time and circadian phase for overall, work and free days. Pointwise bands show uncertainty. A diagonally striped vertical band in the phase panels marks the DLMO reference."
#| fig-cap: "Near-eye exposure grouped by MEQ: clock time (A) and circadian phase (B), overall and by day type. Each curve reports participants and participant-days. Bands are pointwise 95% intervals under the Gaussian reference model. The diagonally striped vertical band marks the DLMO reference."
show_figure("meq_patterns_meq")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-meq-factors
#| fig-alt: "Evening-to-morning exposure factors under MEQ and matched-sample MSFsc classifications, with simultaneous uncertainty bands, counts and a no-difference line at one. Striped vertical bands mark the DLMO reference in the circadian-phase panels."
#| fig-cap: "Evening-to-morning factors for MEQ and MSFsc classifications on identical observations. Panels report participants / participant-days for both sides. Bands use 10,000 coefficient draws, include smoothing-parameter uncertainty, and cover all three day contexts and times at 95% within each coordinate and classification under the fitted covariance model. The diagonally striped vertical band marks the DLMO reference."
show_figure("meq_factor_comparison")
```

Large factors in the early rising portion of the phase curve occur at low absolute exposure. For example, at 2.5 hours after MSFsc, the overall MEQ curves estimate approximately **0.17 lx** for morning participants and **2.94 lx** for evening participants. The factor compares **melanopic EDI + 0.1**, so it is not an unshifted lux ratio. The factor plot should be read alongside the intensity plot.

The Gaussian reference bands identify a candidate overall MEQ interval from 1.25 to 3.58 hours after MSFsc. There is no supported interval in the published DLMO reference interval. The [candidate-window table](results/tables/meq_candidate_windows.csv) provides circular interval boundaries, directions, magnitudes, and the participants, participant-days, and half-hours observed inside each interval. Claims are withheld wherever either direction has fewer than five contributing participants; overall comparisons require that support in both work and free-day cells. Time-varying support is retained in the [curve data](results/tables/meq_all_curves.csv) and [contrast data](results/tables/meq_all_contrasts.csv).

Site composition also limits this comparison. Only MPI has at least five participants in each MEQ direction, and four sites contribute only one direction. Adjusting for site cannot supply the missing within-site comparisons. The sensitivity is therefore evidence about this smaller pooled sample, not a separate confirmation of a general MEQ effect.

@tbl-meq-sites shows the site composition of the retained MEQ groups.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-meq-sites
#| tbl-cap: "Site support for the MEQ sensitivity. Each cell gives participants / participant-days / valid half-hours."
show_table(table_data("meq_site_support") |>
  mutate(sample = paste(participants, participant_days, half_hours, sep = " / ")) |>
  select(site, meq_direction, sample) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = meq_direction, values_from = sample,
              values_fill = "0 / 0 / 0"))
```

The [paired MSFsc pattern figure](results/figures/meq_patterns_msfsc.pdf), [sample registry](results/tables/meq_sample_registry.csv), [diagnostic tables](https://github.com/tscnlab/ZaunerSpitschan_JBiolRhythms_2026/tree/main/results/diagnostics), [acceptance checks](results/provenance/meq_acceptance.csv), and [complete analytical code](R/meq.R) accompany this section. The entry point is `Rscript --vanilla R/meq.R`; cached fits are reused when their data and specification signatures agree.

## Exploratory phase-response weighting {#sec-phase-response}

Daily exposure can occur at phases when light tends to advance or delay the circadian clock. We weight the primary model's estimated near-eye phase curves for the **extreme morning and extreme evening groups** by a published light phase-response curve (PRC) and sum the contributions over 24 hours. This exploratory index is a conceptual comparison of exposure across the advance and delay regions of that PRC, not a prediction of phase shifts. An ambulatory precedent multiplied transformed personal light exposure by the Khalsa PRC and integrated the advance and delay regions [@arguellesprieto2022]. That study used a nonlinear intensity–response transformation and a wrist-temperature phase anchor; here we use modelled log melanopic exposure and MSFsc-relative timing.

### Published curve and phase alignment

We use the PRC from @sthilaire2012, who measured DLMO shifts after a one-hour pulse of approximately 8,000 photopic lux of white light in 18 participants. The numerical coordinates come from the [CSV deposited with their analysis](https://github.com/arcascope/amplitude-simulations/blob/a7abd407f656284a8ae6e8f3490789d2dcda2372/hilaire_12_Fig3A_digitized_data.csv) [@walch2025amplitude]. These authors had digitized the published figure. We use their numerical file without extracting an image ourselves; it is not the original raw dataset. The [local source record](input-data/phase_response/source_manifest.json) fixes the repository version and coordinate definitions.

The figure repeats observations across its circular boundary. We retain one 24-hour interval containing 18 responses, verify that the other ten coordinates are periodic copies, and add 0.5 hours to convert pulse onset to pulse midpoint. A two-harmonic, 24-hour curve is fitted in R. The reusable [PRC helper](R/phase_response.R) defines the import, integration and sensitivity calculations; the calls below execute them at this point in the report.

```{r}
#| label: phase-response-source
source("R/phase_response.R")
prc_source <- phase_response_read_prc()
c(source_participants = nrow(prc_source$points),
  minimum_shift_hours = prc_source$minimum_shift,
  maximum_shift_hours = prc_source$maximum_shift)
```

The fitted extrema round to **−1.75 and +0.45 hours**, matching the published extrema. Positive response values indicate advances and negative values delays. The study measured phase before and after the light pulse using dim-light constant routines. Its no-net-light-response reference of **−0.54 hours** allows for the assumed free-running delay across the three-day measurement interval, based on a mean intrinsic period of 24.18 hours. We compare the **published raw PRC**, $K(u)=P(u)$, with the **drift-corrected PRC**, $K(u)=P(u)+0.54$, where $P(u)$ is the reconstructed curve at pulse midpoint $u$ relative to DLMO.

We align DLMO at **6.45 hours before MSFsc**, the midpoint of the published group-average reference interval, and repeat the calculation at its endpoints, **6.95 and 5.95 hours before MSFsc**. Two wider offsets, 8.45 and 4.45 hours before MSFsc, are additional stress tests. @fig-phase-response-kernel shows both PRC baselines at the central alignment, with markers for DLMO and MSFsc, axes for both time coordinates, and the two primary phase intervals.

```{r}
#| label: fig-phase-response-kernel
#| fig-alt: "Published raw and drift-corrected light phase-response curves, with 18 source points. A gold marker anchors DLMO at 6.45 hours before MSFsc, and a blue marker anchors MSFsc at zero. Bottom and top axes show pulse midpoint relative to MSFsc and DLMO, respectively. Grey windows with dashed boundaries mark the two primary MeLiDos phase intervals. The striped band spans the published DLMO reference interval."
#| fig-cap: "One-hour bright-light PRC fitted to previously digitized coordinates for 18 participants in St Hilaire et al. (2012). The dashed curve retains the published raw baseline; the solid curve adds 0.54 hours for drift correction. Both are shown before weight normalization. The pulse-midpoint coordinate is anchored to the central DLMO reference and MSFsc. Grey windows with dashed boundaries mark the two primary MeLiDos phase intervals. Points come from the PRC study."
phase_response_kernel_figure(prc_source)
show_figure("phase_response_kernel")
```

### Weighted exposure indices

For each extreme group $g$ and day-type context $c$, let $\hat\eta_{gc}(x_j)$ be the primary-model estimate of $\log_{10}(\mathrm{melanopic\ EDI}+0.1)$ at MSFsc-relative phase $x_j$. At ten-minute spacing, $\Delta=1/6$ hour, we calculate

$$
\begin{aligned}
w_j(d)&=\frac{K(x_j-d)\Delta}{\sum_j |K(x_j-d)|\Delta},\\
I_{gc}(d)&=\sum_j w_j(d)\{\hat\eta_{gc}(x_j)+1\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $d$ is DLMO relative to MSFsc. **Zero-exposure centering** subtracts $\log_{10}(0+0.1)=-1$, so the integrated curve is $\hat\eta_{gc}+1$. The positive denominator rescales the sum without changing its sign; the unnormalized signed integral is also exported. The curves retain the primary model's common photoperiod distribution, with site, participant and day effects excluded. Overall curves use the same pooled work/free-day mixture as the main analysis.

The PRC weights have a nonzero signed sum, so the index depends on the PRC baseline as well as the timing of exposure. We compare the published raw and drift-corrected PRCs using the same zero-exposure reference.

We integrate the model design vectors before calculating uncertainty, retaining covariance across phase and between groups. The 95% coefficient intervals use the full covariance with smoothing-parameter correction. They are unadjusted and conditional on the fitted PRC and assumed alignment. They do not propagate uncertainty in the external PRC fit or individual DLMO.

```{r}
#| label: phase-response-integrate
prc_result <- phase_response_integrate(
  prc_source,
  readRDS("results/models/primary_phase.rds"),
  readRDS("results/data/primary_phase_inference.rds")
)
prc_result$checks |> count(passed, name = "checks")
```

```{r}
#| label: phase-response-exports
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Export PRC results and prepare figures"
phase_response_export(prc_result)
phase_response_figures(prc_result)
```

@fig-phase-response-indices compares the two PRC baselines. At the central alignment, the published raw PRC gives zero-exposure-centered overall indices of **−0.15 for extreme morning and +0.05 for extreme evening**, with both intervals including zero. With drift correction, the corresponding estimates are **1.28 and 1.42**. Both intervals exclude zero, indicating advance-weighted exposure (@tbl-phase-response-overall).

```{r}
#| label: fig-phase-response-indices
#| fig-alt: "Two panels compare extreme morning and evening PRC-weighted indices across overall, work and free days, using zero-exposure centering. The left panel uses the published raw PRC and has intervals spanning zero. The right panel uses the drift-corrected PRC and has positive intervals for both groups. Morning-evening intervals overlap in both panels."
#| fig-cap: "PRC-weighted indices for extreme morning and evening groups at the central DLMO alignment, with 95% coefficient intervals. Both panels use zero-exposure centering; the left uses the published raw PRC and the right the drift-corrected PRC. The extreme groups comprise 70 participants, 390 participant-days and 18,066 half-hours; the unchanged four-quartile model uses 140 participants, 778 days and 35,949 half-hours. Positive indices are advance-weighted exposure balances, not phase shifts in hours."
show_figure("phase_response_indices")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-phase-response-overall
#| tbl-cap: "Overall PRC-weighted indices at the central DLMO alignment, centered at zero exposure, with 95% coefficient intervals. Extreme morning: 36 participants, 200 days and 9,241 half-hours. Extreme evening: 34 participants, 190 days and 8,825 half-hours."
prc_overall <- table_data("phase_response_overall_report") |>
  arrange(factor(prc_baseline, c("Published raw", "Drift corrected")), quartile) |>
  mutate(group = paste(extremity, direction),
         interval = sprintf("%.3f to %.3f", lower, upper)) |>
  select(prc_baseline, group, estimate, interval)
show_table(prc_overall, labels = c(prc_baseline = "PRC baseline",
  group = "Group", estimate = "Index",
  interval = "95% CI"))
```

At the central DLMO alignment, the estimates consistently place the extreme evening exposure pattern in a **more phase-advancing direction** than the extreme morning pattern across overall, work and free days and under both PRC baselines. The direct group differences are not statistically significant. The overall evening-minus-morning difference is **0.198 (95% CI −0.094 to 0.491)** with published raw weights and **0.146 (−0.106 to 0.398)** with drift-corrected weights. All group-contrast intervals include zero at the central alignment. Across the three alignments within the published reference interval (5.95, 6.45 and 6.95 hours before MSFsc), the only exception is the work-day contrast with published raw weights and zero-exposure centering at DLMO = −6.95 hours: **0.297 (95% CI 0.001–0.593)**. Overall contrasts remain uncertain under every combination. @tbl-phase-response-contrasts shows the central-alignment results.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-phase-response-contrasts
#| tbl-cap: "Extreme-evening minus extreme-morning PRC-weighted contrasts at the central alignment, centered at zero exposure, with 95% coefficient intervals. Context-specific group samples are shown in the preceding figure; the fitted model and samples are identical under both PRC baselines."
prc_contrasts <- table_data("phase_response_contrast_report") |>
  mutate(interval = sprintf("%.3f to %.3f", lower, upper)) |>
  select(prc_baseline, context, estimate, interval)
show_table(prc_contrasts, labels = c(prc_baseline = "PRC baseline",
  estimate = "Difference", interval = "95% CI"))
```

The absolute balance depends on the drift convention and alignment. Neither PRC baseline gives a clearly separated overall morning–evening index within the published reference interval. Thus these results provide no clear support for an advancing exposure pattern in extreme evening types paired with a delaying pattern in extreme morning types. The laboratory pulse response is not calibrated for summing naturally varying daily melanopic exposure, so these indices cannot be read as hours of phase advance or delay.

The [complete index results](results/tables/phase_response_summary.csv), [group contrasts](results/tables/phase_response_contrasts.csv), [time-specific contributions](results/tables/phase_response_components.csv), and [PRC weights](results/tables/phase_response_weights.csv) retain the alignment and PRC-baseline sensitivities, with zero-exposure centering throughout. The [source guide](input-data/phase_response/README.md), [fitted coefficients](results/provenance/phase_response_fitted_coefficients.csv), [input checksums](results/provenance/phase_response_inputs.csv), and [R session](results/provenance/phase_response_session.txt) document reproduction. The standalone entry point is `Rscript --vanilla R/run_phase_response.R`.

### Sensitivity: advance-to-delay exposure balance

As a sensitivity, we use the broad phase regions of @emens2009. Their advance-to-delay balance divides mean log-transformed exposure from **16 to 4 hours before DLMO** by the mean from **4 hours before to 8 hours after DLMO**. Both regions span 12 hours. We apply their transformation to the fitted near-eye curves, $L_g(x)=\max\{10^{\hat\eta_g(x)}-0.1,0\}$, and calculate the ratio of the two regional means of $\log_{10}\{L_g(x)+1\}$. This is a transformation of the existing fitted exposure curves, rather than a refit with a different response. The overall curves retain the common photoperiod distribution and work/free-day mixture. The calculation uses equal weights within each region and does not use the shape or drift correction of the published PRC.

We retain joint uncertainty across time and groups through **10,000 coefficient draws** with smoothing-parameter correction. The 95% percentile intervals are conditional on the fitted model and assumed DLMO alignment, without multiplicity adjustment. We calculate the central alignment at 6.45 hours before MSFsc and repeat it at 5.95 and 6.95 hours, overall and separately for work and free days. The [calculation helper](R/emens_balance.R) also verifies that averaging the six four-hour bins used by Emens and colleagues gives the same balance as the ten-minute grid.

```{r}
#| label: emens-balance-calculate
source("R/emens_balance.R")
emens_result <- emens_balance(
  readRDS("results/models/primary_phase.rds"),
  readRDS("results/data/primary_phase_inference.rds")
)
emens_result$checks |> count(passed, name = "checks")
```

```{r}
#| label: emens-balance-export
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Export advance-to-delay sensitivity results"
emens_balance_export(emens_result)
```

At the central alignment, the advance-to-delay balance was **2.43 (95% CI 1.94–3.06)** for extreme morning types and **4.28 (3.23–5.71)** for extreme evening types. The evening/morning ratio of these balances was **1.76 (1.21–2.58)**, indicating a higher relative concentration of exposure in the advance region in evening types (@tbl-emens-balance). Its interval excluded one at all three alignments, overall and on work and free days. This broad-region summary supports the direction of the main PRC comparison, whose overall group-contrast intervals included zero. The two methods apply different temporal weights and transformations, and neither estimates a phase shift in hours.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-emens-balance
#| tbl-cap: "Emens-style advance-to-delay balance at the central DLMO alignment. The first two rows divide the advance-region mean by the delay-region mean; the final row compares those balances between groups. Intervals are 95% coefficient-draw percentile intervals. Extreme morning: 36 participants and 200 days; extreme evening: 34 participants and 190 days."
emens_report <- bind_rows(
  emens_result$summary |>
    filter(context == "Overall", dlmo_offset == -6.45) |>
    mutate(comparison = paste("Extreme", tolower(direction))) |>
    select(comparison, estimate, lower, upper),
  emens_result$contrasts |>
    filter(context == "Overall", dlmo_offset == -6.45,
           contrast == "Evening / morning") |>
    mutate(comparison = "Evening / morning balance") |>
    select(comparison, estimate, lower, upper)
) |>
  mutate(interval = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", lower, upper)) |>
  select(comparison, estimate, interval)
show_table(emens_report, digits = 2,
  labels = c(comparison = "Comparison", estimate = "Ratio", interval = "95% CI"))
```

The [complete balances](results/tables/emens_balance_summary.csv), [direct group comparisons](results/tables/emens_balance_contrasts.csv), and [phase-region definitions](results/tables/emens_balance_regions.csv) include all three alignments and day-type contexts. The [standalone R script](R/run_emens_balance.R), [input checksums](results/provenance/emens_balance_inputs.csv), and [runtime record](results/provenance/emens_balance_runtime.txt) document reproduction.

## Comparison with Goulet and colleagues {#sec-comparison-goulet}

### The question shared by the two studies

@goulet2007 explored whether morning and evening types encounter different light patterns when exposure is expressed in clock time or relative to measured circadian phase. That distinction also motivates this analysis. In both studies, the phase comparison tests whether a clock-time difference reflects a shift of the whole daily pattern or a difference that remains after alignment.

The earlier study analysed nine morning and ten evening participants after data-quality exclusions. In the full sample, morning types received more light in the morning and evening types more light late at night. Aligning the observations to measured DLMO removed a statistically detectable group-by-time difference in that full sample. The important exception was the subset with extreme DLMO timing: four morning and five evening participants. In that subset, morning types had higher exposure during much of the three hours before to three hours after DLMO, and evening types had higher exposure 10–12 hours after DLMO. The intermediate-DLMO subset did not show a statistically detectable group-by-time interaction [@goulet2007, pp. 153–156].

“Intermediate” and “extreme” in that comparison described DLMO timing within participants already selected as morning or evening types by MEQ. They were not MEQ severity categories or MSFsc quartiles. The two studies therefore address related questions with different group definitions.

### Design differences and what they contribute

@tbl-study-comparison shows which differences strengthen the present analysis and which limit direct comparison.

The sensor-placement comparison uses the context-specific errors in momentary exposure reported from concurrent MeLiDos recordings by @zauner2026placement.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-study-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Study designs, analytical samples, strengths and limitations."
show_table(table_data("study_comparison"), stub = "feature",
  labels = c(feature = "Feature", goulet = "Goulet and colleagues",
             melidos = "This analysis",
             interpretation = "Consequence for interpretation"))
```

Both studies concern observed personal exposure rather than a controlled change in light. Goulet and colleagues interpreted the extreme-DLMO result as compatible with differences in intrinsic circadian period, but did not measure intrinsic period. The association could also reflect differences in behaviour and available light. Likewise, an association between day length and the MeLiDos contrasts does not establish which exposure caused a chronotype or which behavioural response produced the exposure.

### Similarities, differences and the strength of the conclusions

Both analyses show that clock-time and phase-aligned patterns answer different questions, and that the more extreme groups can show clearer separation. Goulet and colleagues reported two phase-specific findings in their extreme subset: higher morning-type exposure around DLMO and higher evening-type exposure 10–12 hours after DLMO. Our candidate evening-higher difference around 1 to 4 hours after MSFsc is qualitatively compatible with their later-phase finding. We have no supported interval overlapping the published DLMO reference interval (@tbl-windows-direction), although exposure is lower for extreme evening types before the reference interval, which is also qualitatively consistent with that study. The reference interval does not locate each participant's DLMO, so these results cannot establish precise temporal agreement or resolve the earlier near-DLMO finding.

The main strengths here are the larger analytical sample, measurements of melanopic exposure near the eyes, explicit work/free-day comparisons, individual daily curves, and prediction assessed on held-out observations. The earlier study's main strength is its direct measurement of DLMO after a week with relatively stable preferred sleep schedules. Its extreme-phase finding rests on a small selected subgroup, while the present analysis is limited by its sleep-based phase coordinate and uneven site composition.

## Reproducibility and outputs

All counts originate from the shared observation registry. Participants are counted uniquely across day types. Individual plots show their contributing days, model and diagnostic tables show the full analytical sample, and validation separates training from assessment counts.

@tbl-acceptance summarizes the primary acceptance checks.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-acceptance
#| tbl-cap: "Acceptance checks for data joins, time coordinates, AR boundaries, contrasts, counts, Shapley totals and validation separation."
acceptance <- table_data("acceptance_checks", "results/provenance")
show_table(acceptance |> count(passed, name = "checks"))
stopifnot(all(acceptance$passed))
```

The imported data also reproduce in a temporary project without access to the source repository. Eight portability checks confirm unchanged observations, cutoffs, participant metadata and counts. The additional analyses check their samples, classifications, time coordinates, support and displayed counts. An independent daylight verification also checks the constrained basis, direct predictions, interval counts and training-only preprocessing. The [numerical verification](results/provenance/revision7_verify.R) checks 95% simultaneous coverage within each coordinate, reconstructs the primary interval-average contrasts with the full covariance, and verifies the interval definitions used by the photoperiod summaries and manuscript figures. It also confirms that the fitted models, prepared observations and validation inputs are unchanged. The [inference refresh script](results/provenance/revision7_inference.R) regenerates these results from the saved fits.

@tbl-extension-checks summarizes the checks for the additional analyses, and @tbl-versions records the computational environment.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-extension-checks
#| tbl-cap: "Checks for standalone data preparation and the additional analyses."
extension_checks <- bind_rows(
  table_data("standalone_checks", "results/provenance") |> mutate(analysis = "Standalone inputs"),
  table_data("meq_acceptance", "results/provenance") |> mutate(analysis = "MEQ sensitivity"),
  table_data("noncyclic_sz_clock_acceptance", "results/provenance") |> mutate(analysis = "Noncyclic group-curve sensitivity"),
  table_data("noncyclic_sz_phase_acceptance", "results/provenance") |> mutate(analysis = "Noncyclic group-curve sensitivity"),
  table_data("noncyclic_sz_comparison_acceptance", "results/provenance") |> mutate(analysis = "Noncyclic group-curve sensitivity"),
  table_data("daylight_acceptance_checks", "results/provenance") |> mutate(analysis = "Daylight exploration"),
  table_data("daylight_independent_checks", "results/provenance") |> mutate(analysis = "Original daylight fit verification"),

  table_data("revision5_analysis_checks", "results/provenance") |> mutate(analysis = "PRC and photoperiod model verification"),

```

The [imported-data manifest](input-data/manifest.csv), [analysis input manifest](results/provenance/inputs.csv), [source manifest](results/provenance/analysis_sources.csv), [session information](results/provenance/session-info.txt), and [complete acceptance results](results/provenance/acceptance_checks.csv) record provenance. The prepared inputs are byte-for-byte copies of source commit `a5ca7e6e9968e3ca904528a2638f215dfbbd0212`, copied on 22 October 2026. The [input guide](input-data/README.md) explains their roles and retained licensing and citation records.

The OpenMP preload enables `gratia`'s `mvnfast` dependency on this machine. The installed `mgcv` build reports that its own OpenMP support is unavailable, so `bam()` computation runs on one thread. This runtime warning does not indicate a failed model fit.

The full pipeline is invoked with `Rscript --vanilla run.R all`, followed by a fresh Quarto render. The [README](README.md) describes resumable stages and the local OpenMP preload used by gratia. The helpers are [data preparation](R/data.R), [models](R/models.R), [inference](R/inference.R), [diagnostics and individual curves](R/diagnostics.R), [validation](R/validation.R), [attribution](R/attribution.R), [sensitivity checks](R/sensitivity.R), and [figures](R/plots.R). The [histogram section](notes/chronotype-distributions.qmd) is included directly in this document; its [standalone verification](R/chronotype_distributions.R) executes the same code and checks its plotted bin counts. The [gt helper](R/report_tables.R) supplies repeated table formatting. All tables, figure data, fitted models, and diagnostics remain inside this secondary-analysis project.

For display changes alone, `Rscript --vanilla run.R figures` regenerates these figures from saved fits and inference. Model-scale CSV columns remain available alongside the lux and factor columns. Residual diagnostics and predictive scores retain the fitted model's log scale.
